title: Low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing
authors: Yunxin Tang, Zixuan Huo, Junxiang Huang, Zhou You, Zhirao Wang, Zhenai Ding, Yumeng Zeng, Yangyu Lu, Yiming Huang, Zongkang Zhang, Haipeng Xie, Ying Li, Jinzhao Sun, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao
abstract: The execution of useful quantum algorithms on fault-tolerant processors requires more than a mapping from logical gates to encoded operations: the spatial organization, non-Clifford resource supply, and execution schedule must also be determined while keeping physical overhead within practical limits. Although the theoretical hierarchy from logical circuits to fault-tolerant operations is well established, these implementation choices are often specified and optimized separately. Here we develop a low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing. From hierarchical algorithm descriptions, it constructs dependency-preserving logical schedules and an executable workload capturing logical interactions, operation parallelism, and time-resolved non-Clifford demand, thereby linking logical computation to surface-code organization, resource-state preparation, and fault-tolerant execution in a traceable workflow. We apply the framework to twenty benchmark circuits across seven algorithm families and a hierarchically composed application-scale elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm workload. Physical costs vary substantially even for circuits with similar logical resource counts. Under our direct-rotation calibration, non-Clifford implementation selection reduces space-time volume by up to 241.5 times versus an all-synthesis baseline for the QAOA amplitude-amplification workload. Circuit-specific surface-code layouts reduce routed-latency estimates for all twenty benchmarks; thirteen also reduce space-time volume because communication savings outweigh added spatial overhead. These results show that low-cost fault-tolerant execution depends on computation scheduling and organization, not aggregate logical resource counts alone.
summary: This paper presents a novel, low-cost framework that bridges the gap between abstract quantum algorithms and physical execution on surface-code quantum computers. By creating an 'executable workload' representation, it accounts for scheduling, resource supply, and spatial organization simultaneously. The results prove that optimizing the execution structure, rather than just the logical gate count, is key to achieving practical, low-overhead quantum computation.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a low-cost, end-to-end framework to translate high-level quantum algorithms into concrete, physically constrained execution schedules for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
main_result: The framework demonstrates that low-cost execution depends critically on computation scheduling and organization, achieving significant reductions in space-time volume (up to 241.5 times) compared to baseline methods.
method: The authors introduce an 'executable workload' intermediate representation that captures logical interactions, parallelism, and time-resolved non-Clifford demand, linking the algorithm to physical resource requirements.
model_or_system: The work is specifically tailored for surface-code quantum computing, requiring the determination of spatial organization and resource supply alongside the logical circuit execution.
key_observables: Physical overhead, routed-latency estimates, space-time volume, logical interaction structure, and time-resolved non-Clifford demand.
important_parameters: The comparison between circuit-specific layouts versus standardized baselines, and the scale of the benchmark circuits (twenty benchmarks across seven families).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the execution cost is determined by the scheduling and organization of operations, not just the aggregate count of logical resources.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the workflow from high-level algorithms through the executable workload representation to the final physical surface-code layout, comparing optimized vs. standardized approaches.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of current separate optimization stages, then introducing the executable workload as a unifying intermediate representation, and finally applying this framework to benchmark circuits to quantify cost savings.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial algorithmic tool for quantum hardware engineers and theorists, moving beyond abstract circuit depth to address the practical, resource-constrained scheduling necessary for near-term fault-tolerant devices.
